lesson.title: Widening the Guess to Show Your Uncertainty
lesson.summary: An interval estimate reports a range of plausible values for a parameter instead of a single number, giving an honest picture of how much uncertainty surrounds the estimate.
lesson.body:
A point estimate answers the question "what is your best guess?" An interval estimate answers a more honest question: "what is a range of values that plausibly contains the true parameter?" Instead of reporting a single number like p-hat equals 0.25, an interval estimate reports something like the true proportion is plausibly somewhere between 0.21 and 0.29. That range communicates precision, or the lack of it, in a way a bare point estimate cannot.

The general structure of an interval estimate is always the same: take the point estimate, and add and subtract some cushion that reflects how much the statistic tends to vary from sample to sample. Wider cushions produce wider, more cautious intervals, narrower cushions produce tighter, riskier ones. The next several chapters build this cushion piece by piece: first the standard error, which measures typical sampling variability, then a critical value, which sets how many standard errors of cushion to use, then the margin of error, which multiplies the two together, and finally the confidence interval itself, which is the point estimate plus and minus that margin of error.

The reason interval estimates matter so much in practice is that they force honesty about uncertainty. A headline reporting "62% of voters support the measure" sounds precise, but a poll of 400 people cannot pin down a population proportion to the exact percentage point. Reporting an interval, such as 58% to 66%, communicates the actual resolution of the data, which is a more truthful and more useful piece of information for anyone trying to make a decision based on it.

Using the transit survey data from the last two chapters, p-hat equals 0.25 from n equals 400, it is possible to build a 95% interval estimate for p once you know how to compute the cushion. Working that cushion out precisely takes the next three chapters, but the completed answer, computed with the standard tools this unit builds, turns out to be the interval from about 0.2075 to 0.2925, or 20.75% to 29.25%. Instead of committing to the single number 25%, this interval communicates the genuine range of plausible values for the true population proportion, given a sample of this size. The rest of this unit is devoted to showing exactly how that interval gets built, and precisely what "95%" means when attached to it.
